\chapter{Age, and And}
\label{ch:zh-sui-he}
\hlchaptermodality{27}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say how old I am in a sentence with no verb in it, and join two nouns with \zh{和} while knowing it may not join two sentences.}

\zh{岁} gives the numerals their first thing to measure, and \zh{和} is the first joining word this track has ever had — one that teaches where it may not go.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[suì]{\zh{岁} — six strokes, and a rule that is not left-to-right}

\label{lesson:ZH-W27-sui}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter, and its first character breaks a habit.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nǐ ne — duì bu duì} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ne} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{de} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ma} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shénme} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — a mountain, then an evening}
\begin{quote}
\zh{岁}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Six strokes}, three on top and three beneath.

The top is \zh{山} \emph{shān}, a mountain — and it is written in an order the rules you have been given do not predict:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{shù} down the \textbf{middle}
  \item the \textbf{shùzhé} — down the left side, then turn and run along the base
  \item the \textbf{shù} down the right side
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Centre before the sides.} Every character so far has gone top before bottom and left before right, and those two rules decide almost everything in Chinese writing. \zh{山} is where they run out, and the answer is a third rule: when a shape has a clear middle and two wings, the middle goes first.

The bottom is \zh{夕} \emph{xī}, an evening:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item a short \textbf{piě} falling to the lower left
  \item the \textbf{héngzhégōu}, turning down and falling to the lower left with a hook
  \item the \textbf{diǎn} dot laid across it
\end{enumerate}

Top before bottom holds between the halves, as always.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{山} — middle first, then left, then right
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{岁} — \zh{山} on top, \zh{夕} beneath
  \item \emph{Cover:} write \zh{岁} from memory
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes does \zh{岁} have? (\textbf{Six}.) Which stroke of \zh{山} comes first? (\textbf{The middle one}.) What sits underneath? (\textbf{\zh{夕}}, an evening.)

Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%B2\%81.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{岁}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[suì]{\zh{岁} — how old you are}

\label{lesson:ZH-C27-sui}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and the numerals finally do something.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{suì} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ne} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{de} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ma} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shénme} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{岁}} \emph{suì} is \textbf{fourth tone} — the sharp fall, like \zh{四} and \zh{对}.

It counts \textbf{years of age}, and only that. It is not the word for a year on a calendar.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{十八岁}} \emph{shíbā suì} — eighteen years old \textbf{\zh{二十岁}} — twenty \textbf{\zh{九十九岁}} — ninety-nine
\end{quote}

Every one of those numbers came from the decimal chapter, and until this word there was nothing for them to measure.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the sentence with no verb in it}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我十八岁}} \emph{wǒ shíbā suì} — I am eighteen.
\end{quote}

Read that again and look for the verb. \textbf{There is none.} No \zh{是}, no anything. Subject, number, \zh{岁}, stop.

English needs \emph{am}. Spanish needs \emph{tengo}. Mandarin puts an age straight after the person and is finished — and putting \zh{是} in is a mistake a beginner makes for months: \emph{\zh{我是十八岁}} is wrong.

The question is built the same way, with \zh{吗} doing what it always does:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{你十八岁吗}} — are you eighteen?
\end{quote}

And now three things this book taught separately can be said in one breath:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我是中国人} — \zh{我有一个名字} — \zh{我十八岁}}
\end{quote}

Name, nationality, age — the three pieces of personal information any beginner's paper asks for, and the last of them was waiting on this one character.

\textbf{One habit worth knowing.} Mandarin asks a small child's age with one question and an adult's with another, and both need words this book has not taught yet. What this lesson gives you is the answer, which is the half you are asked for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{shíbā suì} — \zh{十八岁}
  \item \zh{我十八岁} — and hear that there is no verb
  \item \zh{你十八岁吗}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \zh{岁} count? (\textbf{Years of age}.) What verb does \zh{我十八岁} use? (\textbf{None} — there is no verb in it.) What is the commonest beginner's mistake here? (\textbf{Putting \zh{是} in}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hé]{\zh{和} — eight strokes, and the right half is a mouth}

\label{lesson:ZH-W27-he}



\begin{quote}
Two lessons in, and three of these eight strokes are already yours.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{suì} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{duì} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn shū de rén} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{me} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — \zh{禾} first, then \zh{口}}
\begin{quote}
\zh{和}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Eight strokes}, five on the left and three on the right — and the three on the right are \zh{口}, which you have written since the fourth chapter.

The left half is \zh{禾} \emph{hé}, standing grain:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item a short \textbf{piě} at the very top, falling left
  \item the \textbf{héng} beneath it
  \item the long \textbf{shù} straight down the middle
  \item a \textbf{piě} falling to the lower left
  \item a \textbf{diǎn} closing to the lower right
\end{enumerate}

Then \zh{口}, in its usual order:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{shù} down its left side
  \item the \textbf{héngzhé} across the top and down the right
  \item the \textbf{héng} closing the floor
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Left half complete before the right one starts}, as always.

This is a \textbf{phono-semantic compound}, the kind the \zh{请} lesson named: one part carries meaning and the other carries sound. Here the sounding half is unusually generous — \zh{禾} is itself said \emph{hé}, so the character tells you its own pronunciation outright.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{禾} — then \zh{和}, with \zh{口} on the right
  \item \emph{Cover:} write \zh{和} from memory
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes does \zh{和} have? (\textbf{Eight} — five plus \zh{口}'s three.) Which half supplies the sound? (\textbf{\zh{禾}}, which is itself \emph{hé}.) Which earlier character worked the same way? (\textbf{\zh{请}}.)

Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%92\%8C.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{和}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hé]{\zh{和} — and, between things only}

\label{lesson:ZH-C27-he}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and this word opens a column this book has never had.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hé} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{duì} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Hànyǔ, wǒ kàn shū} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kànjiàn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shén} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{和}} \emph{hé} is \textbf{second tone} — the rise, the same shape as \zh{十} and \zh{人}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{你和我}} \emph{nǐ hé wǒ} — you and I \textbf{\zh{书和名字}} — books and names \textbf{\zh{中国人和学生}}
\end{quote}

It stands between the two things and joins them. Nothing agrees, nothing changes, and it is the same word however many things there are.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it joins nouns, and only nouns}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{和} joins two nouns. It does NOT join two sentences.}
\end{quote}

This is the part an English or Spanish speaker gets wrong on the first day, because in their language one word does both:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Right:} \textbf{\zh{我和你}} — you and I \emph{(two nouns)} \textbf{Wrong:} \emph{\zh{我看书和你看书}} — not Mandarin at all
\end{quote}

English says \emph{I read and you read}. Spanish says \emph{yo leo y tú lees}. Mandarin will not use \zh{和} there at all. To join two statements it simply \textbf{puts them next to each other}, with a comma and no joining word:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我看书} — \zh{你看书}} — I read, and you read.
\end{quote}

Mandarin writes a comma at that seam; this book prints a dash, because it has taught no punctuation. What matters is that \textbf{there is no joining word in it at all.} That is not a shortcut or a casual register — it is how Mandarin does it, and the words that DO join clauses are different words for different relations, \emph{because}, \emph{but}, \emph{or}, none of which is \zh{和} and none of which this book has yet taught.

\textbf{So \zh{和} is the first joining word in this track}, and the first thing it teaches is where it may not go.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nǐ hé wǒ} — \zh{你和我}
  \item \zh{书和名字}
  \item \zh{我看书} — \zh{你看书} — two sentences, no \zh{和}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \zh{和} join? (\textbf{Two nouns}.) What does it never join? (\textbf{Two sentences}.) How does Mandarin join two statements instead? (\textbf{It puts them side by side}, with a comma.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\zh{我十八岁} — \zh{你和我}}

\label{lesson:ZH-C27-practice}



\begin{quote}
The chapter closes on two unrelated characters that each open a column.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hé} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nǐ ne — duì bu duì} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ de shū — kàn shū de rén} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kànjiàn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ shì} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — an age, and a join}]
Two characters, fourteen strokes, and each one opens something the track has never had.

\textbf{\zh{岁}} gives the numerals something to measure. The decimal chapter reached ninety-nine and had nothing to count; \zh{我十八岁} is the first sentence in this book that uses a number to say something true about a person — and it does it with no verb at all.

\textbf{\zh{和}} is the first joining word in the whole track. It joins two nouns and it refuses two sentences, and knowing the refusal is most of the lesson.

Put them together with what you already have:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我是中国人} — \zh{我有一个名字} — \zh{我十八岁}} \textbf{\zh{你和我是学生}}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Listen.} \emph{Wǒ shíbā suì. Nǐ hé wǒ shì xuésheng.}

\textbf{Speak.} Give your age with no verb; then join two people with \zh{和}.

\textbf{Read.} \zh{我十八岁} — \zh{你和我是学生}

\textbf{Write.} \zh{岁} — \zh{山} middle-first, then \zh{夕}. \zh{和} — \zh{禾}, then \zh{口}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{我十八岁}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{你和我是学生}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{岁} \zh{和}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What verb does an age sentence use? (\textbf{None}.) What does \zh{和} join, and what does it refuse? (\textbf{Nouns; sentences}.) Which stroke of \zh{山} comes first? (\textbf{The middle one}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
